description: Strings in the Wolfram Language are atomic objects manipulated by a family of String* functions that all accept string patterns: literal strings, the symbolic StringExpression algebra, character classes, or RegularExpression. This category covers construction, extraction, searching, replacement, case and padding operations, conversion between strings and expressions, and templating.

tools.name: StringJoin
tools.description: Concatenates strings, written infix with the <> operator. It flattens lists of strings, so StringJoin[{"a", "b"}] works as well as StringJoin["a", "b"]. All arguments must be strings; use ToString first for numbers and other expressions.
tools.usage:
StringJoin[s1, s2, ...]
s1 <> s2
StringJoin[{s1, s2, ...}]
tools.example:
"Hello, " <> "world!"
StringJoin[{"a", "b", "c"}]
"file" <> ToString[3] <> ".txt"
StringJoin[Riffle[{"x", "y"}, ", "]]
tools.notes: For joining many strings with a separator, StringRiffle is clearer and avoids building intermediate lists.

tools.name: StringLength
tools.description: Gives the number of characters in a string, counting Unicode code points rather than bytes. It is Listable, so it maps automatically over a list of strings. Use it instead of Length, which gives 0 for any string because strings are atoms.
tools.example:
StringLength["hello"]
StringLength[{"a", "abc"}]
StringLength["caf\[EAcute]"]
SortBy[words, StringLength]

tools.name: StringTake
tools.description: Extracts a substring by character position, using the same specifications as Take: n for the first n characters, -n for the last n, and {m, n} for a range. Negative indices count from the end and a step may be given as {m, n, s}. It is the direct way to slice fixed-width fields.
tools.usage:
StringTake[string, n]
StringTake[string, -n]
StringTake[string, {m, n}]
StringTake[string, {{m1, n1}, {m2, n2}}]
tools.example:
StringTake["abcdefg", 3]
StringTake["abcdefg", -2]
StringTake["abcdefg", {2, 4}]
StringTake["2024-05-17", {1, 4}]
tools.notes: Asking for more characters than the string has raises a message; use StringTake[s, UpTo[n]] for a lenient version.

tools.name: StringDrop
tools.description: Returns a string with characters at the specified positions removed, using the same index forms as Drop. StringDrop[s, n] removes the first n characters and StringDrop[s, -n] the last n. It is the complement of StringTake.
tools.example:
StringDrop["abcdefg", 2]
StringDrop["report.txt", -4]
StringDrop["abcdef", {2, 3}]
tools.notes: StringDelete removes characters matching a pattern rather than at fixed positions, and FileBaseName is a better choice for stripping extensions.

tools.name: StringSplit
tools.description: Splits a string into a list of substrings at whitespace by default, or at occurrences of a given string pattern. A list of delimiters splits at any of them, and a rule delimiter -> value keeps the delimiters in the output. The option IgnoreCase and a count argument limiting the number of pieces are both supported.
tools.usage:
StringSplit[string]
StringSplit[string, delim]
StringSplit[string, {d1, d2, ...}]
StringSplit[string, delim, n]
tools.example:
StringSplit["a b  c"]
StringSplit["a,b,c", ","]
StringSplit["a1b22c", DigitCharacter ..]
StringSplit["k=v", "=", 2]
StringSplit["a, b; c", {",", ";"}]
tools.notes: Empty pieces between adjacent delimiters are dropped by default; use StringSplit[s, d -> d] or a RegularExpression when you need to keep them.

tools.name: StringReplace
tools.description: Replaces occurrences of string patterns with new text, taking a single rule or a list of rules tried in order at each position. The right-hand side may be a function of the named pattern variables when RuleDelayed is used. Options include IgnoreCase and a maximum number of replacements.
tools.usage:
StringReplace[string, s -> t]
StringReplace[string, {r1, r2, ...}]
StringReplace[string, rules, n]
StringReplace[rules][string]
tools.example:
StringReplace["hello world", "world" -> "there"]
StringReplace["a1b2", DigitCharacter -> "#"]
StringReplace["abc", x_ /; LetterQ[x] :> ToUpperCase[x]]
StringReplace["2024-05-17", RegularExpression["(\\d+)-(\\d+)"] :> "$2/$1"]
tools.notes: Replacement scans left to right and does not reconsider text it has already produced, so rules never loop. Use StringReplacePart for position-based edits.

tools.name: StringCases
tools.description: Returns the substrings that match a string pattern, optionally transformed by a rule. It is the extraction workhorse: named pattern variables in a StringExpression become available on the right-hand side, so parsing and reformatting happen in one step. Options include Overlaps, IgnoreCase and a limit on the number of matches.
tools.usage:
StringCases[string, patt]
StringCases[string, patt -> rhs]
StringCases[string, patt, n]
StringCases[patt][string]
tools.example:
StringCases["a1b22c", DigitCharacter ..]
StringCases["x=1, y=2", l_ ~~ "=" ~~ d_ :> {l, d}]
StringCases["abcabc", "a" ~~ _ ~~ "c"]
StringCases[text, RegularExpression["[A-Z][a-z]+"]]
ToExpression /@ StringCases["12 and 34", NumberString]
tools.notes: Matches never overlap unless Overlaps -> True is given. StringExtract and StringPosition cover the positional variants.

tools.name: StringMatchQ
tools.description: Tests whether an entire string matches a string pattern, returning True or False. Because the match must cover the whole string, it is the right test for validating identifiers, filenames and formats. It supports shell-style metacharacters (* and @) in plain string patterns and the IgnoreCase option.
tools.usage:
StringMatchQ[string, patt]
StringMatchQ[string, patt, IgnoreCase -> True]
StringMatchQ[patt][string]
tools.example:
StringMatchQ["hello", "h" ~~ __]
StringMatchQ["data.csv", "*.csv"]
StringMatchQ["ABC", "abc", IgnoreCase -> True]
Select[files, StringMatchQ["*.txt"]]
StringMatchQ["12345", DigitCharacter ..]
tools.notes: Use StringContainsQ for a substring test; StringMatchQ anchors at both ends.

tools.name: StringContainsQ
tools.description: Tests whether a string contains a match for a pattern anywhere within it. It is the modern, readable replacement for StringFreeQ negation and for checking substring membership. Lists of alternatives, IgnoreCase and the operator form are all supported.
tools.example:
StringContainsQ["hello world", "world"]
StringContainsQ["abc", DigitCharacter]
Select[lines, StringContainsQ["ERROR"]]
StringContainsQ["Hello", "hello", IgnoreCase -> True]

tools.name: StringStartsQ
tools.description: Tests whether a string begins with a given pattern, with StringEndsQ as the mirror test for suffixes. Both accept lists of alternatives and the IgnoreCase option, and both have operator forms that work directly inside Select and Cases. They are the clear way to filter by prefix or file extension.
tools.example:
StringStartsQ["filename.txt", "file"]
StringEndsQ["filename.txt", ".txt"]
Select[names, StringStartsQ["Dr."]]
StringStartsQ["HTTP://x", "http", IgnoreCase -> True]

tools.name: StringFreeQ
tools.description: Returns True when a string contains no match for the given pattern, the logical complement of StringContainsQ. It is convenient as a filter that keeps items lacking a marker, for example lines without a comment character. Lists of patterns and IgnoreCase are supported.
tools.example:
StringFreeQ["hello", "z"]
Select[lines, StringFreeQ["#"]]
StringFreeQ["abc123", DigitCharacter]

tools.name: StringPosition
tools.description: Gives the {start, end} character positions of every match of a string pattern. The results can be fed to StringTake or StringReplacePart for position-based editing. Overlaps -> False suppresses overlapping matches and a count argument limits how many are reported.
tools.usage:
StringPosition[string, patt]
StringPosition[string, patt, n]
StringPosition[string, patt, Overlaps -> False]
tools.example:
StringPosition["abcabc", "bc"]
StringPosition["aaa", "aa"]
StringPosition["aaa", "aa", Overlaps -> False]
StringTake["abcabc", First[StringPosition["abcabc", "ca"]]]

tools.name: StringCount
tools.description: Counts how many times a pattern matches in a string, without building the list of matches. It is faster and clearer than Length[StringCases[...]] for tallies. Overlaps and IgnoreCase options work as in StringPosition.
tools.example:
StringCount["mississippi", "ss"]
StringCount["a1b2c3", DigitCharacter]
StringCount[text, WordBoundary ~~ "the" ~~ WordBoundary]

tools.name: StringInsert
tools.description: Inserts a string at a given character position, with negative positions counting from the end and a list of positions inserting in several places at once. Positions refer to the original string, so multiple insertions do not shift each other. It is useful for formatting fixed-layout text.
tools.usage:
StringInsert[string, snew, n]
StringInsert[string, snew, {n1, n2, ...}]
tools.example:
StringInsert["abcd", "-", 3]
StringInsert["abcd", "X", -1]
StringInsert["12345678", " ", {3, 5, 7}]

tools.name: StringDelete
tools.description: Removes every substring matching a pattern, equivalent to replacing it with the empty string but more direct. It accepts a list of patterns and the IgnoreCase option, and has an operator form for pipelines. Use it to strip punctuation, tags or whitespace.
tools.example:
StringDelete["a-b-c", "-"]
StringDelete["h3ll0", DigitCharacter]
StringDelete[html, "<" ~~ Shortest[__] ~~ ">"]
StringDelete[{"a.txt", "b.txt"}, ".txt"]

tools.name: StringReverse
tools.description: Reverses the order of characters in a string. It is Listable, so it maps over lists of strings automatically. Use it for palindrome tests and simple text transformations; Reverse does not work on strings because they are atoms.
tools.example:
StringReverse["abcdef"]
StringReverse[{"ab", "cd"}]
palindromeQ[s_] := s === StringReverse[s];
palindromeQ["racecar"]

tools.name: ToUpperCase
tools.description: Converts all letters in a string to upper case, following Unicode case mapping, and is Listable over lists of strings. ToLowerCase is the complementary function, with Capitalize and LetterQ covering related needs. Case folding respects accented characters.
tools.example:
ToUpperCase["hello"]
ToUpperCase[{"a", "b"}]
ToUpperCase["caf\[EAcute]"]
Capitalize["hello world"]

tools.name: ToLowerCase
tools.description: Converts all letters in a string to lower case using Unicode case mapping. It is the usual normalization step before comparing or tallying words. Like ToUpperCase it is Listable.
tools.example:
ToLowerCase["HeLLo"]
Counts[ToLowerCase /@ TextWords[text]]
Sort[DeleteDuplicates[ToLowerCase[words]]]
tools.notes: Most String* functions also accept IgnoreCase -> True, which avoids the need to normalize case first.

tools.name: StringTrim
tools.description: Removes whitespace from both ends of a string, or removes whatever matches a given pattern at the ends. It is the standard cleanup applied to fields read from files or user input. Only the leading and trailing matches are removed; interior text is untouched.
tools.example:
StringTrim["  hello  "]
StringTrim["xxhelloxx", "xx"]
StringTrim[#, "\""] & /@ fields
StringTrim["000123", "0" ..]

tools.name: StringPadLeft
tools.description: Pads a string on the left to a specified total length, using spaces by default or a supplied padding string. StringPadRight is the right-aligned counterpart. Both truncate when the string is already longer than the requested width, which makes them suitable for fixed-width table output and zero-padded numbers.
tools.usage:
StringPadLeft[string, n]
StringPadLeft[string, n, padding]
StringPadRight[string, n, padding]
tools.example:
StringPadLeft["7", 3, "0"]
StringPadLeft["ab", 5]
StringPadRight["name", 10, "."]
StringPadLeft[ToString[#], 4, "0"] & /@ {1, 22, 333}
tools.notes: IntegerString[n, 10, digits] is a more direct way to produce fixed-width zero-padded integers.

tools.name: StringRiffle
tools.description: Joins a list of strings into one, inserting separators between them, with a three-argument form supplying left and right delimiters as well. Nested lists are joined with different separators for rows and elements, which makes it a one-liner for CSV or TSV text. Non-string elements are converted with ToString automatically.
tools.usage:
StringRiffle[list]
StringRiffle[list, sep]
StringRiffle[list, {left, sep, right}]
StringRiffle[nested, {rowsep, colsep}]
tools.example:
StringRiffle[{"a", "b", "c"}]
StringRiffle[{"a", "b"}, ", "]
StringRiffle[{1, 2, 3}, {"[", "; ", "]"}]
StringRiffle[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, "\n", ","]

tools.name: StringTemplate
tools.description: Creates a reusable template object from a string containing `slot` or <* expression *> markers, which are filled in by applying the template to arguments or an Association. It handles escaping, defaults and inserted Wolfram Language expressions, making it the right tool for generating text, SQL, HTML or reports. TemplateApply evaluates a template against data in one call.
tools.usage:
StringTemplate["text with `slot`"]
template[assoc]
template[arg1, arg2]
StringTemplate[str][<|"key" -> val|>]
tools.example:
t = StringTemplate["Hello, `name`! You are `age`."];
t[<|"name" -> "Ada", "age" -> 36|>]
StringTemplate["`1` + `2` = `3`"][1, 2, 3]
StringTemplate["Sum is <* Total[Range[10]] *>"][]
tools.notes: Use TemplateSlot and TemplateExpression for programmatic construction, and FileTemplate to apply a template stored in a file.

tools.name: TemplateApply
tools.description: Applies a template expression or template object to supplied parameters and returns the filled-in result. It works on StringTemplate objects, on expressions containing TemplateSlot, and on FileTemplate and XMLTemplate objects. Use it when the template and the data arrive separately.
tools.example:
TemplateApply[StringTemplate["x = `x`"], <|"x" -> 5|>]
TemplateApply[TemplateExpression[TemplateSlot[1] + 1], {10}]
TemplateApply["Value: `1`", {42}]

tools.name: ToString
tools.description: Converts any expression to a string in the specified output form, InputForm and TextString being the usual choices. ToString[expr] uses OutputForm, which is fine for display but may lose precision or structure; ToString[expr, InputForm] produces text that can be read back with ToExpression. Formatting options such as NumberMarks and PageWidth control the result.
tools.example:
ToString[123]
ToString[x^2 + 1]
ToString[x^2 + 1, InputForm]
ToString[N[Pi, 20], InputForm]
"n=" <> ToString[42]
tools.notes: For round-tripping always use InputForm; ToString[1.0] gives "1." in OutputForm which may not parse as intended elsewhere. TextString gives human-readable text for dates, quantities and entities.

tools.name: ToExpression
tools.description: Parses a string as Wolfram Language input and evaluates it, optionally in a different input form such as TeXForm or StandardForm. A third argument supplies a wrapper such as Hold so the parsed expression is not evaluated. It is how you turn configuration text, user input or file contents into live expressions.
tools.usage:
ToExpression[string]
ToExpression[string, form]
ToExpression[string, form, h]
tools.example:
ToExpression["2 + 3"]
ToExpression["x^2", InputForm, Hold]
ToExpression["\\frac{1}{2}", TeXForm]
ToExpression /@ StringSplit["1,2,3", ","]
tools.notes: Evaluating arbitrary strings is unsafe with untrusted input; use Interpreter, ImportString[..., "JSON"] or Internal`StringToDouble for parsing data values.

tools.name: Characters
tools.description: Splits a string into a list of one-character strings. It is the entry point for character-level processing with the ordinary list functions, and StringJoin reverses it. For character codes use ToCharacterCode instead.
tools.example:
Characters["hello"]
Counts[Characters["mississippi"]]
StringJoin[Reverse[Characters["abc"]]]
ToCharacterCode["AB"]

tools.name: CharacterRange
tools.description: Gives the list of characters in a Unicode code-point range, specified either by characters or by integer codes. CharacterRange["a", "z"] is the standard way to build an alphabet. Combine with Tuples or RandomChoice to generate identifiers and test data.
tools.example:
CharacterRange["a", "e"]
CharacterRange["0", "9"]
CharacterRange[945, 969]
StringJoin[RandomChoice[CharacterRange["a", "z"], 8]]
tools.notes: Alphabet[] and Alphabet["Greek"] give ready-made alphabets for many languages.

tools.name: RegularExpression
tools.description: Wraps a PCRE-style regular expression so it can be used anywhere a string pattern is expected. Capture groups are referred to as "$1", "$2" in replacement strings, or bound to variables through StringCases with a rule. Use it when a regex is more compact than the symbolic StringExpression form.
tools.example:
StringCases["a1b22", RegularExpression["[0-9]+"]]
StringReplace["2024-05-17", RegularExpression["(\\d{4})-(\\d{2})"] -> "$2/$1"]
StringMatchQ["abc123", RegularExpression["[a-z]+\\d+"]]
StringSplit["a, b ,c", RegularExpression["\\s*,\\s*"]]
tools.notes: Backslashes must be doubled inside Wolfram Language strings. StringExpression patterns are often more readable and can embed arbitrary Wolfram conditions.

tools.name: StringExpression
tools.description: The symbolic string pattern algebra, written infix with the ~~ operator, that concatenates literal strings, blanks, character classes and pattern objects. It supports the full pattern machinery including named variables, Alternatives, Repeated, Condition and Except, so patterns can call arbitrary Wolfram Language tests. Every String* function accepts a StringExpression wherever a pattern is expected.
tools.usage:
s1 ~~ s2 ~~ ...
StringExpression[s1, s2, ...]
x : patt ~~ ...
tools.example: StringCases["key=value", k__ ~~ "=" ~~ v__ :> {k, v}] StringMatchQ["abc123", LetterCharacter .. ~~ DigitCharacter ..] StringReplace["a.b", "." ~~ x_ :> ToUpperCase[x]] StringCases["hi", "<" ~~ Shortest[tag__] ~~ ">"]
tools.notes: Default matching for __ inside string patterns is shortest-first at each position; wrap in Longest when you need greedy behaviour.

tools.name: DigitCharacter
tools.description: A string pattern object matching a single decimal digit 0-9, with the complementary class available as Except[DigitCharacter]. Combined with Repeated it matches numbers, as in DigitCharacter ... It is the readable alternative to the regex class \d.
tools.example:
StringCases["a12b3", DigitCharacter ..]
StringMatchQ["12345", DigitCharacter ..]
StringDelete["h3ll0", DigitCharacter]
StringSplit["ab12cd", DigitCharacter ..]
tools.notes: HexadecimalCharacter, NumberString and Interpreter["Number"] cover richer numeric parsing needs.

tools.name: LetterCharacter
tools.description: A string pattern object matching a single letter, including accented and non-Latin letters under the Unicode definition. Use it with Repeated for words and with Except to match non-letters. LetterQ is the corresponding predicate for testing an existing character.
tools.example:
StringCases["ab12cd", LetterCharacter ..]
StringMatchQ["Hello", LetterCharacter ..]
StringDelete["a1!b2", Except[LetterCharacter]]
LetterQ["x"]

tools.name: WordCharacter
tools.description: A string pattern object matching a letter or digit, corresponding to the regex class \w without the underscore. WordBoundary matches the zero-width position between a word and non-word character, which lets you match whole words. Together they make word-level extraction straightforward.
tools.example:
StringCases["a_1 b2", WordCharacter ..]
StringCases[text, WordBoundary ~~ "the" ~~ WordBoundary]
StringSplit["one-two three", Except[WordCharacter] ..]

tools.name: TextWords
tools.description: Splits text into a list of words using linguistic rules rather than plain whitespace, correctly handling punctuation, contractions and non-Latin scripts. A second argument limits how many words are returned, and a rule form can keep the separators. It is the right starting point for word frequency analysis.
tools.example:
TextWords["Hello, world! It's fine."]
Length[TextWords[article]]
ReverseSort[Counts[ToLowerCase /@ TextWords[text]]]
tools.notes: Use TextSentences for sentence segmentation and TextCases for entity extraction.

tools.name: TextSentences
tools.description: Splits text into sentences using linguistic boundary detection, so abbreviations and decimal points do not cause false breaks. A count argument returns only the first n sentences, which is handy for previews and summaries. It works on strings and on imported documents.
tools.example:
TextSentences["One. Two! Three?"]
TextSentences["Dr. Smith arrived. He waited."]
TextSentences[Import["article.txt"], 3]

tools.name: StringForm
tools.description: Formats a string by substituting arguments into numbered slots written as `` `1` ``, `` `2` `` or a bare `` ` `` for successive arguments. It is the traditional way to build message text, and is what Message uses internally for messages defined with ::usage-style templates. The result is a formatted object; wrap it in ToString to get a plain string.
tools.example:
StringForm["x = `1`, y = `2`", 3, 4]
ToString[StringForm["file `` of ``", 2, 10]]
f::bad = "Bad value `1`.";
Message[f::bad, 7]
tools.notes: StringTemplate is the modern alternative with named slots, defaults and embedded expressions; StringForm remains standard for message definitions.

tools.name: StringRepeat
tools.description: Repeats a string a given number of times, optionally truncating or padding the result to an exact length. It replaces the older StringJoin[Table[...]] idiom and is useful for building separators and indentation. The two-argument form gives exactly n copies; the three-argument form gives a result of exactly the requested length.
tools.example:
StringRepeat["ab", 3]
StringRepeat["-", 40]
StringRepeat["abc", 5, 7]
tools.notes: Available in Wolfram Language 13.1 and later; in earlier versions use StringJoin[ConstantArray[s, n]].
